source.title: A Mechanistic Study of Transformers Training Dynamics
source.authors: Ambroise Odonnat; Wassim Bouaziz; Vivien Cabannes

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some plots and equations are flattened in the web text, but the relevant accuracy figures are described in the text.
record.tranche_reason: The study trains a small transformer on sparse modular addition and examines its accuracy and circuit formation, but it does not reproduce the original grokking setup or its measures of delayed generalization.
record.gate_note: The study reports train/test accuracy dynamics and examines how circuits form, so those results bear on V1, V2, and V6. References to other works' findings are excluded. The study does not report results on memorizing-component removal, weight decay or critical dataset size, realistic large-model grokking, or optimizer/numerical controls for a grokking delay.
record.test_reason: The study never studies grokking or delayed generalization. Training uses 2048 samples, train and test accuracy rise together, and there is no memorization phase, no weight decay, no data-size sweep and no optimizer controls. Its one result bearing on a version is qualitative: on sparse modular addition, trained one-block transformers realise different variants of a clustering-head circuit, and which variant depends on initialization. This bears on V6 (same algorithm across runs) in a new, non-grokking setting.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct as paraphrased. Transformers can solve sparse modular addition via clustering heads, which are stationary points of the loss and emerge in practice, with variations. Training is two-stage (embedding clustering, then MLP fitting) via saddle-point escape, and loss spikes stem from the high curvature of normalization and feed-forward layers. The authors present this as a sandbox for intuition about LLM training stability.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses a one-block question-answering transformer trained on sparse modular addition and focuses on circuit visualizations and training stability. It does not reproduce the original grokking experiment or the mechanistic progress measures from the cited grokking work.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors report that exit from saddle points and test accuracy vary with batch size, hidden dimension, learning rates, and MLP learning-rate discount. They also report that initialization affects circuit realizations and that pretraining on p = 2 facilitates subsequent p = 3 training.

fits_no_version.finding: Learning proceeds in two abrupt loss drops: sequence-embedding clustering, then MLP fitting. The drops coincide with gradient-norm peaks, read as escape from saddle points, and the escape time varies strongly with hyperparameters.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Abrupt, stage-wise learning in small transformers on algorithmic tasks reflects saddle-point escape, with train and test improving together.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 1st International Conference on Machine Learning Mechanistic Interpretability Workshop, PMLR 306, 2026
record.problems: The study is a controlled study of a single transformer block and is not a grokking-delay replication. Accuracy trajectories relevant to the delay are shown in plots without numerical values or a textual account of whether training accuracy saturates before test accuracy rises. Circuit results are largely qualitative and include illustrative cases. The text reports substantial hyperparameter sensitivity and high variability in test accuracy.
record.rows_left_out: No additional results bearing directly on the listed claim versions were omitted. The sparsity-versus-performance experiments, transfer accuracy sweeps, and loss-spike analyses were not included as rows because they do not measure the behaviors named by the tested versions.

untested.parts: No memorization-then-generalization delay, no data-size sweep.
No generalizing vs memorizing circuits, no progress measures.
No non-algorithmic data and no initialization-scale or weight-norm sweep.
No weight decay or efficiency account, no critical dataset size, no ungrokking.
No comparison across architectures. Frequencies of each circuit variant are not quantified; only d=2 illustrations and the p=3 transfer result.
No optimizer or floating-point controls on a grokking delay. Loss spikes from normalization curvature are not grokking.

missing.what: The final attention pattern correlates with the attention pattern at initialization, so initialization shapes the circuit's concrete realization.
Across 250 runs of transfer from p=2 to p=3, only models with the full six-cluster clustering head (not the partial or fuzzy variants) reached 100% test accuracy.

record.verdict_notes: The paper does not mention grokking beyond citing Power et al., Nanda et al. and Liu et al. It is linked only weakly to V6, through qualitative circuit-variant observations. Its loss-spike analysis concerns training instability, not grokking artifacts (V7).

versions.untested_parts: The study does not report perfect training accuracy while test accuracy remains at chance, quantify a long delay after overfitting, or compare delay across training-set sizes.
It does not measure removal of memorizing components or continuous progress measures that anticipate a grokking jump.
No non-algorithmic datasets or initialization-scale/weight-norm sweep testing a lazy-to-rich transition.
No LLM pretraining or fine-tuning on realistic data.
No test of weight decay or another low-norm bias as an efficiency account, critical dataset size, or ungrokking.
The study describes varied circuit realizations, but does not systematically identify and compare algorithms across architectures and hyperparameter settings.
No test of adaptive-optimizer instabilities or floating-point softmax limits as causes of grokking delays, or controlled demonstration that such a delay disappears.

rows.subject: single-block transformer (d = 2; illustrative run)
rows.operation_detail: Track train and test accuracy during sparse modular addition training.
rows.measure: Train and test accuracy over training
rows.value: figure only; the text says both train and test accuracy increase as the model improves
rows.note: The description establishes improvement in both accuracies but does not specify whether test accuracy stays at chance after training accuracy saturates or whether there is a long delay.
rows.check: There is no overfitting regime and no delay is measured; the text says train and test accuracy increase together. This is not a V1 measurement.

rows.subject: single-block transformer (illustrative run)
rows.operation_detail: Visually track sequence embeddings and the feed-forward classifier during training.
rows.measure: Order and character of circuit learning
rows.value: The sequence embeddings become clustered after the first loss drop; a second loss drop follows as the MLP fits a classifier to the clusters. The MLP weights are described as evolving continuously.
rows.note: This reports staged circuit formation, but not removal of memorizing components or continuous progress measures anticipating a delayed-generalization jump.
rows.check: The two-stage learning (embedding clustering, then MLP fit) involves no memorizing components, no their removal and no progress measure anticipating a delayed jump, so it does not bear on V2. Record it under fits_no_version.

rows.subject: trained transformer (illustrative model)
rows.operation_detail: Inspect sequence-embedding clusters for learned input invariances.
rows.measure: Whether sequence embeddings capture suffix and permutation invariances
rows.value: Some illustrated models lack invariance to a suffix token and to permutations of non-spurious tokens, producing more clusters than the idealized circuit.
rows.note: The authors describe incompletely learned invariants and a circuit that differs from the idealized construction.
rows.check: Partially learned invariants are a variant of the clustering head that fails to capture some invariances. This bears on algorithm uniformity (V6), not on V2.

source_check.locator_found: Section 4.1; Section 4.2, Partially learned invariants; Figure 3.

rows.subject: trained transformer (illustrative model)
rows.operation_detail: Inspect an alternative clustering of sequence embeddings.
rows.measure: Generalization of an unconventional circuit realization
rows.value: The text says fuzzy constructions use unconventional patterns and nonetheless generalize to unseen data.
rows.note: This is an observed alternative to the idealized circuit, not evidence that a grokking delay occurred.
rows.check: In the fuzzy construction an occasional run generalizes with an unconventional clustering rather than the clustering head. This is evidence against a single shared algorithm, not evidence on V2.

source_check.correct: state=partial for V6. Occasionally, unconventional clustering patterns generalize to unseen data. The authors describe these within variations of the idealized circuit; they do not establish that a shared algorithm is absent.
source_check.locator_found: Section 4.2, opening paragraph and Fuzzy constructions; Figure 4; Remark B.3.
source_check.problem: The absent state overstates evidence from unconventional circuit realizations within a broadly shared clustering approach.

rows.subject: trained transformer (illustrative model)
rows.operation_detail: Inspect attention and value transformations in a trained circuit.
rows.measure: Whether the resulting sequence embeddings remain invariant to the suffix
rows.baseline: attention fully concentrated on the informative tokens
rows.value: The value matrix collapses embeddings of attended spurious tokens, allowing sequence embeddings to remain suffix-invariant.
rows.note: This is a varied implementation of the circuit operation; it does not establish that all runs use the same identifiable algorithm.
rows.check: Faulty attention corrected by the value matrix is a different implementation of the same clustering-head operation. This bears on V6 only.

source_check.locator_found: Section 4.2, Faulty attention corrected by value; Figure 2.
